Even a brilliant technologist can mess up. Bill Gates was a brilliant technologist when he cofounded Microsoft , but he has never managed to completely integrate Microsoft into the world, and its share price has collapsed in response to poor results. And so the question arises: what would have happened if the company had kept Gates out of it from the start? To find out, IBM scientists in Cambridge, Massachusetts set up a computerized e-mail server in 2004, which was designed to test whether the e-mail server could be programmed to respond to an e-mail from a different user. In the end, this test succeeded. So what did the researchers do? They wrote an e-mail from Gates with a message from himself, which would never have been sent. target: modern man in the Philippines is not exactly the same as day in the life of a modern man in the United States, much less a man from the Middle East. That's not to say that globalization is bad. It is, and will continue to be, an important factor in Philippine culture, just as it’s been in the United States for centuries. But, it creates a different experience in the lives of those in the Philippines who are born and raised there. It is, in this sense, a “global” experience, one that has a more or less universal appeal. And so the Philippines began to change, and to be changed, from one generation to the next. In many ways, the development of modern Manila began before globalization itself. input: IT alligator tales I grew up in New York, where giant alligators -- sometimes more ornately described as albino alligators -- were rumored to roamIT Myth 5: Most IT projects fail Do most IT projects fail? Some point to the number of giant consultancies such as IBM Global Services, Capgemini
target: , and Accenture. IT consulting firms have made a fortune, and they attract a lot of criticism. But the facts don't match myth The big problem with IT is that it is often difficult to measure success. For IT, it is the cost of the services that matters. That can lead to very poor projects with high project costs. IT is also very large. According to a recent study by the McKinsey Institute, more than 60% of the IT organization has more than 100,000 employees. A survey by IBM found that more than half of those IT organizations have more than 500 employees, with many more people in operations and infrastructure. IT is expensive, and it's hard to measure success. The largest IT consulting firms, including those cited above, do have success stories. But they are not as successful as companies such as IBM. IBM spends around $6 billion on consulting services per year. That seems like a lot of money. However, the consulting firm's clients are relatively small.

target:
red object in the night sky, I asked my husband what he thought.

The answer? "I don't know what the hell that is." I have never heard anyone describe Venus as red.

It is actually a brilliant blue-black star, with a red light emitted by its atmosphere. It's not really known how the planet Venus is seen to vary in brightness with its passage in and out of the Sun over a series of months. Venus has not orbited the Sun in the past 12,000 years, so we have no records. And it's only in the past few hundred years or so that scientists became interested in Venus' proximity to the Sun, and started studying its atmosphere with spacecraft like the European Space Agency's Venus Express and NASA's Venus Express and Pioneer Venus Express missions.

But Venus has changed since the early days of human exploration of the Solar System. During the 1970s, when Venus was first discovered, the planet's atmosphere was relatively thick.

input: Italy's Pennetta Wins Idea Prokom Open (AP) AP - Italy's Flavia Pennetta won the Idea Prokom Open for her first WTough Race Ahead for Swimmer Phelps  ATHENS (Reuters) - Michael Phelps, his first gold medal  safely gathered in, eased through the next
target: stage of his Olympic career with a time more than a second faster than the second place finisher in the 100 meters butterfly on Saturday. The gold was Phelps' sixth and his first medal at the Games, his fifth in a row  and gave him a total of nine golds, eight silvers and two bronze medals since swimming's debut at the 1900 Paris Games. It also was Phelps' second gold medal in the event in the past three Olympics, after winning it in 2004. The 24-year-old, who is now the most decorated Olympian in history with six golds and eight medals overall, finished in 51.61. He was one hundredth of a second faster than the second place finisher in the 100 butterfly.  Phelps was in his fifth Olympics, his first since 2008 and his first outside the United States. He was also competing at his sixth Olympics. His performance Saturday was more than a second better than the first place finisher in the 100 fly this year.

That compares with $4.8 billion for executive salaries and $5.8 billion for executive bonuses a year earlier, and represents little change from the previous survey.
The Washington area's top compensation, including bonuses, rose by nearly 7 percent in dollar terms from a year ago, when it fell in real terms, the survey showed, while salary and bonuses fell by nearly 8 percent in real terms.
"We saw a year with fewer executive bonuses, and pay rises for those that were given," said Joe Dawson, director of research and consultancy services for Thomson Reuters/Freelance.
"Companies were more willing to give them and companies were rewarding them for growth than they have been in the past."

WASHINGTON — Spending at the Pentagon rose 5.4 percent last year, up from 4.3 percent the previous year, as military programs were boosted by a $1 trillion increase in Defense Department outlays.

The Pentagon’s spending grew to $612.8 billion, according to data from the Pentagon released Thursday. And while that’s the highest yearly total on record, the annual growth rate was significantly slower than in past years.

In fact, the spending growth rate was the slowest of the decade. Spending rose 3.9 percent between 2007 and 2009, for example.

The spending increase came from the Pentagon’s massive $1 trillion increase in defense outlays, which grew to $612.8 billion.

One of those problems is that many services are so tightly coupled, the various pieces that make up an application may not work together very well, Micro Focus said.

Micro Focus has a new software service it hopes to help companies overcome this situation: Micro Focus Web services for Microsoft Windows called Boot Services.

Micro Focus Web Services for Microsoft Windows is a new package of plug-ins for Microsoft Windows called Boot Services for Microsoft Windows, aimed at making application integration as straightforward and error-free as possible, Micro Focus said.

"This is unacceptable," said John Schindler, the US government's chief scientist from 1996 to 2002.

He said the ruling was "not without legal consequences" and the United States "will be following the situation closely," he said.

target:
But what about its real estate assets? Well, the deal to acquire the former Sears and Kmart properties, along with other properties and businesses, could be worth roughly $200 million.

"They may wind up having a real big presence in the retail industry, and then they will probably sell off the real estate and build out Kmart's retail footprint, and then they'll probably wind up selling off the real estate and build out Kmart's real estate," Hilzenrath said.

"In the end, Kmart's going to wind up owning their real estate," said Flagg, of The Oregonian/OregonLive.

The deal is expected to be announced by the end of the month, and the first phase of the project is expected to be done by November, Hilzenrath said.

But no one's ever claimed the cave.

target:

The number of butterflies dropped by 62 percent, or more than 5 million, from last year, according to the Illinois Department of Agriculture.

Butterflies have been decimated by the widespread loss of habitat and insects.

Butterflies are a critical, and costly, insect that pollinators and small mammals need, and which, say environmentalists, eat a third of fruit and vegetables, the Illinois Department of Agriculture says.

Experts say that, as climate change alters weather patterns, butterflies and other insects may have fewer places to go in their search for food, water or predators.

"People need to be aware that there will be impacts, and I would say in general people are going to pay more attention to it," said Wilson Ainsworth, director of the Butterfly Program at the University of Illinois Springfield, which has tracked the butterflies since 1976. "There will be positives and negatives, but it's going to change our behavior a bit."

WASHINGTON (AP) — Consumer prices, which have been buffeted this year by soaring energy costs, fell by 0.1 percent in January, the Labor Department reported Thursday, more than the 0.2 percent decline economists had expected.

The drop in the price of energy prices helped offset a drop in prices of clothing, footwear and motor vehicles, along with other categories of food and services. The price for new cars, trucks and sport utility vehicles rose modestly in January, pointing to a slowing in the pace of inflation.

"With consumer prices rising much less than earlier in the year, inflation will be lower in the coming months," said Steven Ricchiuto, chief economist at Barclays Capital. "It's not going to be an overwhelming negative impact."

Consumer prices have been accelerating as fuel costs and food increase.

The plan is for the Jewish homes to be built on land slated to become part of a future Palestinian state. The housing minister will present the plan to cabinet and then Sharon will have 15 days to sign off on it, his office said.

target:
Korean nuclear and missile programs with North Korea, pressing on with a second day of talks that brought together the United States, Russia, China, South Korea and Japan as well as the North.
As U.S. Secretary of State Rex Tillerson continued a trip to China that began on Tuesday, China's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying urged the United States not to abandon its "positive stance."
Asked if China was taking an active part in the talks, Hua said China was making all efforts to "ensure an active and productive outcome," citing recent attempts by U.S. diplomats to meet separately without China's involvement.
The talks were due to resume at 1300 GMT.
The talks were being held in the Chinese city of Dalian to find ways to rein in Pyongyang's nuclear and missile programs.
U.S. and Chinese negotiators were meeting in China to work out details, including an "exchange mechanism" to determine when and where the North Koreans would visit for talks.

Its system uses RFID tags, which are tiny, light-emitting transceivers and are used in the food and agriculture sectors.

The NDS will allow Kanto Denki to print parts more accurately, according to the company. It will also help keep paper records of products and equipment more securely.

input: Rover discovers clues of water on Mars surface After months of crossing a vast Martian crater floor and zigzagging up low-slung hills, NASA #Cassini finds two more Saturn moons NASA #39;s Cassini spacecraft has discovered two new Saturn moons, the smallest yet found among its dozens of natural satellites
target:
.
The spacecraft's latest pictures show the moons Enceladus and Tartarus, orbiting the planet Saturn. Enceladus is a giant ocean world with a dense atmosphere. The Saturnian moon has a large central core with two giant, liquid water reservoirs, which are exposed near the surface. Scientists believe that water is being released on the satellite as the ice is forced out with the passage of time.
The picture shows a series of bright, water-covered features, some of which look like a lake-sized pool of liquid. In another photo taken in June, Enceladus is the brightest part of the image.
"These moons are all incredibly interesting, and I am very pleased to see more of them. I believe this is the highest resolution of the moons to date," said Alan Stern, the principal investigator of NASA's Cassini orbiter. "We are getting amazing images and lots of new information of a world that is so far from Earth."

Bernstein, who was born in Germany and moved to Los Angeles as a teenager, composed the music for more than 60 films during a remarkable half-century career that ranged from action films such as "Jurassic Park" to musicals such as "The Sound of Music" and "Annie" to comedies such as "Forrest Gump."

"We don't know if there are more deaths or if there are more injured," Escobar said.

"We don't know how many gang members we have here," Escobar said.

"We don't know where they are now, but all we know now is that they are taking refuge in the prisons."

The violence erupted on Tuesday when two inmates tried to escape from a prison in San Pedro Sula, the capital city.

The inmates clashed with other inmates at a maximum security prison in central El Salvador, killing 15 and wounding at least 23 others, officials said.

Argentine President Carlos Menem has announced the first of a series of reforms aimed at restoring the country's battered economy.

"Today the first of a series of economic measures will begin - with the aim of putting an end to the current crisis and restoring peace," he said as he opened a cabinet meeting.

The government announced a slew of planned reforms, including the opening of Argentina's borders to foreign tourists and the resumption of imports of Argentine soybeans.

"We want the country to regain stability, security and prosperity," said Menem.

"We want the economy to grow, but without generating instability."

Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund, which lent Argentina more than $55 billion during the crisis and is still in a $57.6 billion recovery program with the country, said it expected a "firm economic recovery" this year.

New Orleans Hornets

The NBA franchise has had a difficult history in New Orleans since purchasing the franchise from the New Orleans Jazz, and was forced into financial distress in April 2011 due to the NBA lockout that left the organization without a home. The Hornets have not made the playoffs since the 2006-07 NBA season. In July, team president and general manager Dave Choate resigned, and current team president Mitch Kupchak assumed the role, with Choate heading back to his home in the Orlando area. The team has been trying to fill Choate's position ever since. The team has moved to its current home, the Smoothie King Center, in June 2013. The team's season ticket sales were up 31 percent in 2012-13 compared to 2011-12 and are expected to rise even more in the 2013-14 season.

target:
playing the game he loves. But this offseason also has brought out a lot of personal demons that got buried, but Fields realized that there's a big difference between healing and simply letting go.
As Fields gets older, his health is beginning to take a greater toll. He was forced to undergo surgery in April to remove a bone spur from his left ankle, and a second operation on his right ankle in October. In the middle of a Super Bowl run last season, he was forced to undergo surgery to remove a bone spur from his left ankle, as well as a stress fracture in his left tibia. He went through a similar situation in the offseason last year. He's also dealing with some lingering pain in his back and hamstring.
For this season, he has replaced former team captain Steve Smith as the starting middle linebacker for the Redskins. The 30-year-old is hoping to keep his career on track, but he said the first part of the season will likely be a struggle.

The verdict in San Jose, Calif., came Thursday against the Houston-based oil giant, which collected only \$3 million in claims against it. The jury ruled that Texaco, now known as Mobil Corp., failed to implement a plan devised by a public-service corporation to deal with the spill and caused "substantial nuisance." "Texaco should have been more concerned with their shareholders than with the citizens of the community," said Judge Michael Chagla of the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Northern District of California. target: , a leading medical journal reported Thursday. "What we were doing there was an atrocity, a barbarity, but we knew it was right to do it," Dr. Michael Gross, who headed a team that treated about 1,200 prisoners at a US military prison at Abu Ghraib in 2002, told the journal The Lancet. An internal US investigation, released earlier this week, concluded that "torture, in some forms, was an appropriate response" to interrogations, but that Gross and other psychiatrists played "an instrumental role in the use of abusive techniques" against detainees. The report by the Office of Inspector General concluded Gross and his colleagues at the Abu Ghraib prison provided inmates with psychological torture, and helped them to make false admissions, in order to keep prisoners from escaping. Gross was a member of a team of doctors at the prison that was supposed to treat prisoners who were under "protective custody," but instead treated those who had been captured and held for interrogation.

input: United signals it may end pensions United Airlines has signaled that it may terminate and replace employee pension plans, a move its parent company says is needed before it can emergeLayoffs at Fleet THE LAYOFFS at Fleet seem to be a microcosm of the economy as a whole. Good, higher-paying, full
target: -time jobs are hard to find. So many people are out of work that good jobs are hard to find. That's created a surplus, and some companies have decided that's a great time to cut back and fire employees. United Continental has been one of them. On Oct. 1, the airline announced that it would layoff 2,700 workers. It would not say what positions would be cut. But the company would not comment further on this week's layoffs except to say that it may no longer have a pension plan for current employees. United was among the first airlines to offer its employees defined-benefit pensions. In the 1980s and 1990s, the federal government required all large companies — including United — to offer pensions to its workers. They were able to keep them even after the companies went bankrupt or went out of business. When the government took over airlines, they were allowed to keep them until they went out of business. However, United has been growing faster than most companies.

Britain's case has been a particular focus because it has the highest number of medals at stake.
